The really interesting thing about building space robots is that the current CPU technologies we have is very sensitive to things like solar flares and radiation.

Performing menial tasks (mining, agriculture, even building railways and roads) has been automated multiple times now - it is safe to say that there is somebody on earth today who knows how to write the software, how to design the robot and the mechanical hardware for performing these tasks. However, the thing that breaks is the computer - a single solar flare can flip a bit and cause all sorts of crazy things to happen.

Keep an eye out for technology designed to be "space-grade". These usually involve having two CPUs running the same program, and some sort of check to ensure both programs came up with the same result (it's very very unlikely that a solar flare would cause the exact same bit flip in both CPUs). Other mechanisms involve building in this fancy math technique called error control coding ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_detection_and_correction ) to try and autocorrect tiny bit flips.

It's a fascinating field, and in my opinion, far more interesting than A.I

For a couple of decades I was very active in the space advocacy community. I spent over a decade working on the updating and elabortion of The Millennial Project and for a time was president of the Living Universe Foundation/First Millennial Foundation. As part of that, I was also working on the development of OTEC based marine facilities as a means to combat Global Warming --seasteading with a practical purpose. But I gave up on the organization when it became clear that space advocacy had devolved into a cargo cult and interest in active participation in anything at all had died in that community. I hold out hope for an amateur space development movement, but see it as now more likely to emerge from the Maker and hobby robotics communities. I've been trying to cultivate interest in an open telerobotics space program based on the development of prototype telebases building on hobby robotics, but haven't yet been able to get things to critical mass alone and find it hard to get others to comprehend the concept without visual examples. It's too divergent from the traditional space vision in our culture, even though the trends in technology have made that vision increasingly anachronistic.

I've since focused more of my interest in Post-Industrial futurism, the Maker, Open Tech/FLOK/FLOSS, P2P, and Commons movements. I'm very interested in 'proactive futurism' (actively cultivating desired futures rather than merely anticipating them) and the notion of the 'living museum of the future'; using the approach of the many 'living museums' showcasing life of the ancient past as a way to illustrate and communicate ideas about life in the future. I think there is great potential in creating design exhibits to showcase future lifestyle and present a positive vision to compete with the compulsively dystopian visions of the media. I've been developing a video documentary project called Open House which would showcase the building of a home and lifestyle based on open source designs and personal digital fabrication. But, again, I can't get things to critical mass alone and find the concept difficult to communicate to others.

Most recently I've started work on a Maker's guidebook to modular building systems. An overview of the various modular building systems whose parts can be easily made or found off-the-shelf and which people can freely use in their own creations. Most DIY enthusiasts have used one or more of these modular building systems, but often know little about them. It's common even for professional engineers to routinely use things like T-slot profile framing without ever having heard the term 'T-slot' before, only knowing these systems in the context of a particular brand they stumbled onto; Bosh, MK, 80:20, etc. I've been collecting information on these building systems for decades, and so thought an overview of them might be an accessible project, though somehow I'm going to have to deal with illustrating them and getting sample components for demonstration builds. I'm hoping there's potential for a sustainable home business in this, perhaps through an online store for parts or the establishment of a Maker design/publishing studio.
